claim: SNARE proteins play a crucial role in intracellular trafficking by catalyzing membrane fusion.
source: SNARE proteins play a crucial role in intracellular trafficking by catalyzing membrane fusion, but assigning SNAREs to specific intracellular transport routes is challenging with current techniques.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by extensive literature.

claim: Assigning SNAREs to specific intracellular transport routes is challenging with current techniques.
source: SNARE proteins play a crucial role in intracellular trafficking by catalyzing membrane fusion, but assigning SNAREs to specific intracellular transport routes is challenging with current techniques.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study and reflects current limitations in the field.

claim: A novel FRET-FLIM-based technique was developed allowing visualization of real-time local interactions of fluorescently tagged SNARE proteins in live cells.
source: We developed a novel Förster resonance energy transfer-fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FRET-FLIM)-based technique allowing visualization of real-time local interactions of fluorescently tagged SNARE proteins in live cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of this technique throughout the Results section.

claim: Activation of dendritic cells by bacterial lipopolysaccharide leads to increased FRET of fluorescently labeled syntaxin 4 with VAMP3 specifically at the plasma membrane.
source: We found that activation of dendritic cells by bacterial lipopolysaccharide leads to increased FRET of fluorescently labeled syntaxin 4 with VAMP3 specifically at the plasma membrane, indicating increased SNARE complex formation, whereas FRET with other tested SNAREs was unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: LPS activation of dendritic cells results in increased SNARE complex formation between syntaxin 4 and VAMP3.
source: We found that activation of dendritic cells by bacterial lipopolysaccharide leads to increased FRET of fluorescently labeled syntaxin 4 with VAMP3 specifically at the plasma membrane, indicating increased SNARE complex formation, whereas FRET with other tested SNAREs was unaltered.
evidence: The increased FRET is interpreted as indicating increased SNARE complex formation.

claim: FRET with other tested SNAREs was unaltered by LPS activation.
source: We found that activation of dendritic cells by bacterial lipopolysaccharide leads to increased FRET of fluorescently labeled syntaxin 4 with VAMP3 specifically at the plasma membrane, indicating increased SNARE complex formation, whereas FRET with other tested SNAREs was unaltered.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM data in Figure 5 showing no significant changes for Stx3 or VAMP8.

claim: SNARE complexing is a key regulatory step for cytokine production by immune cells.
source: Our results revealed that SNARE complexing is a key regulatory step for cytokine production by immune cells and prove the applicability of FRET-FLIM for visualizing SNARE complexes in live cells with subcellular spatial resolution.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observed correlation between increased Stx4-VAMP3 complex formation and IL-6 secretion.

claim: FRET-FLIM is applicable for visualizing SNARE complexes in live cells with subcellular spatial resolution.
source: Our results revealed that SNARE complexing is a key regulatory step for cytokine production by immune cells and prove the applicability of FRET-FLIM for visualizing SNARE complexes in live cells with subcellular spatial resolution.
evidence: The entire study demonstrates this capability through multiple experiments.

claim: All intracellular membrane fusion, except for mitochondrial fusion, is catalyzed by SNARE proteins.
source: One of the central paradigms in cell biology is that all intracellular membrane fusion, except for mitochondrial fusion, is catalyzed by soluble NSF (N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive fusion protein) attachment protein receptor (SNARE) proteins (Hong, 2005; Jahn and Scheller, 2006).
evidence: This is cited as a central paradigm in cell biology with supporting references.

claim: There are about 36 SNARE proteins identified in mammals.
source: There are about 36 SNARE proteins identified in mammals which can be classified in R-SNAREs or Q-SNAREs depending on the central residue of their SNARE motif being either arginine (R) or glutamine (Q).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SNARE proteins.

claim: SNARE proteins can be classified into R-SNAREs or Q-SNAREs depending on the central residue of their SNARE motif being either arginine (R) or glutamine (Q).
source: There are about 36 SNARE proteins identified in mammals which can be classified in R-SNAREs or Q-SNAREs depending on the central residue of their SNARE motif being either arginine (R) or glutamine (Q).
evidence: This is a standard classification system for SNARE proteins.

claim: The interaction of one R motif and three Q motifs (termed Qa, Qb and Qc) of cognate SNARE proteins located in opposing membranes leads to the formation of a 4-helix coiled-coil bundle.
source: The interaction of one R motif and three Q motifs (termed Qa, Qb and Qc) of cognate SNARE proteins located in opposing membranes leads to the formation of a 4-helix coiled-coil bundle.
evidence: This describes the structural mechanism of SNARE complex formation.

claim: Trans-SNARE complex formation brings membranes in close proximity and catalyzes their fusion.
source: This trans-SNARE complex formation brings the membranes in close proximity and catalyzes their fusion.
evidence: This is the established mechanism of SNARE-mediated membrane fusion.

claim: After membrane fusion is complete, the SNAREs are in a cis-conformation and need to be disassembled by the AAA-ATPase NSF in conjunction with α-SNAP.
source: After membrane fusion is complete, the SNAREs are in a so-called cis-conformation and need to be disassembled by the AAA-ATPase NSF in conjunction with α-SNAP (Söllner et al., 1993; Hong, 2005; Jahn and Scheller, 2006).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about the SNARE cycle.

claim: Different intracellular trafficking steps are catalyzed by specific sets of SNARE proteins.
source: From studies in yeast and many mammalian cell types, including neurons, neuroendocrine cells, adipocytes and epithelial cells, it is clear that different intracellular trafficking steps are catalyzed by specific sets of SNARE proteins (Pelham, 2001; Hong, 2005; Jahn and Scheller, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by extensive literature in multiple cell types.

claim: In immune cells, specific combinations of SNARE proteins mediate release of cytokines, chemokines and delivery of surface receptors via specific secretory pathways.
source: Also in immune cells, such as granulocytes, platelets, mast cells, macrophages and T cells, specific combinations of SNARE proteins mediate release of cytokines, chemokines and delivery of surface receptors via specific secretory pathways (Collins et al., 2015; Stow et al., 2009; Stanley and Lacy, 2010; Lacy and Stow, 2011; Murray and Stow, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations about SNARE function in immune cells.

claim: Many SNAREs locate to multiple organelles.
source: However, these approaches suffer from the problems that many SNAREs locate to multiple organelles, as SNAREs are promiscuous and can be involved in different trafficking steps, and that mere co-localization of SNAREs does not prove their actual interaction (Pelham, 2001; Hong, 2005).
evidence: This is cited as a known limitation in studying SNARE localization.

claim: SNAREs are promiscuous and can be involved in different trafficking steps.
source: However, these approaches suffer from the problems that many SNAREs locate to multiple organelles, as SNAREs are promiscuous and can be involved in different trafficking steps, and that mere co-localization of SNAREs does not prove their actual interaction (Pelham, 2001; Hong, 2005).
evidence: This is cited as a known characteristic of SNARE proteins.

claim: Mere co-localization of SNAREs does not prove their actual interaction.
source: However, these approaches suffer from the problems that many SNAREs locate to multiple organelles, as SNAREs are promiscuous and can be involved in different trafficking steps, and that mere co-localization of SNAREs does not prove their actual interaction (Pelham, 2001; Hong, 2005).
evidence: This is cited as a limitation of localization microscopy approaches.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments cannot resolve in which organelle SNARE interactions take place.
source: Interactions can be shown with co-immunoprecipitation experiments, but these cannot resolve in which organelle the interactions take place.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of co-immunoprecipitation methods.

claim: SNAREs are functionally redundant.
source: Perturbation experiments, such as genetic ablation of SNAREs, overexpression of soluble 'dominant negative' SNARE fragments, or microinjection of antibodies directed against SNAREs, are also difficult to interpret because SNAREs are functionally redundant and defects in a specific trafficking route cannot be discerned from upstream trafficking steps.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic that complicates perturbation experiments.

claim: Knockdown or knockout of many SNARE proteins often does not show a clear phenotype.
source: Because of this, knockdown or knockout of many SNARE proteins often does not show a clear phenotype (Hong, 2005; Bethani et al., 2009; Nair-Gupta et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is cited as a consequence of SNARE functional redundancy.

claim: FRET is based on the energy transfer from a donor to an acceptor fluorophore within the Förster distance range.
source: FRET is based on the energy transfer from a donor to an acceptor fluorophore within the Förster distance range.
evidence: This is the fundamental principle of FRET.

claim: FRET leads to quenching of the donor fluorophore and sensitization of the acceptor fluorophore.
source: FRET leads to quenching of the donor fluorophore and sensitization of the acceptor fluorophore and can either be measured from fluorescence intensities (ratiometric FRET) or from a decrease in fluorescence lifetime of the donor fluorophore (FRET-FLIM).
evidence: This describes the observable effects of FRET.

claim: FRET can be measured from fluorescence intensities (ratiometric FRET) or from a decrease in fluorescence lifetime of the donor fluorophore (FRET-FLIM).
source: FRET leads to quenching of the donor fluorophore and sensitization of the acceptor fluorophore and can either be measured from fluorescence intensities (ratiometric FRET) or from a decrease in fluorescence lifetime of the donor fluorophore (FRET-FLIM).
evidence: This describes the two main methods for measuring FRET.

claim: Ratiometric FRET and FRET-FLIM have been previously used to characterize cytosolic interactions of fungal SNAREs.
source: Ratiometric FRET and FRET-FLIM have been previously used to characterize cytosolic interactions of fungal SNAREs (Valkonen et al., 2007) and of the neuronal Qa-SNARE syntaxin 1 (Stx1) and the Qb/c-SNARE SNAP25 (Rickman et al., 2007; Medine et al., 2007; Rickman et al., 2010; Xia et al., 2001; Kavanagh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations of previous work.

claim: The crystal structure of the neuronal SNARE complex revealed that the luminal/extracellular C-termini of VAMP2 and Stx1 are in immediate proximity (<1 nm) after membrane fusion.
source: We hypothesized that FRET-FLIM could also be used to measure full ternary cis-SNARE complex formation, as the crystal structure of the neuronal SNARE complex revealed that the luminal/extracellular C-termini of the R-SNARE vesicle-associated membrane protein 2 (VAMP2) and of Stx1 are in immediate proximity (<1 nm) after membrane fusion (i.e., in the cis-SNARE complex) (Stein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on a cited crystal structure.

claim: In vitro, FRET between VAMP2 and Stx1 can be measured by labeling their C-termini with organic fluorophores.
source: In vitro, FRET between these SNAREs can be measured by labeling their C-termini by means of site-specific labeling with organic fluorophores (Xia et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Degtyar et al. (2013) showed interactions between VAMP2 and Stx1 C-terminally fused to fluorescent proteins by TIRF microscopy combined with ratiometric FRET.
source: In vivo, Degtyar et al. (2013) showed interactions between VAMP2 and Stx1 C-terminally fused to fluorescent proteins by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy combined with ratiometric FRET (Degtyar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct citation of previous work.

claim: Ratiometric FRET is technically challenging as extensive controls are required to correct for local concentration differences of the donor and acceptor fluorophores.
source: However, ratiometric FRET is technically challenging as extensive controls are required to correct for local concentration differences of the donor and acceptor fluorophores (Jares-Erijman and Jovin, 2003; Wallrabe and Periasamy, 2005).
evidence: This is cited as a known limitation of ratiometric FRET.

claim: FLIM does not suffer from concentration-dependent artifacts because the lifetime is an intrinsic characteristic of a fluorophore which is not influenced by the probe concentration nor by the excitation intensity.
source: FLIM does not suffer from this limitation, as the lifetime (τ) is an intrinsic characteristic of a fluorophore which is not influenced by the probe concentration nor by the excitation intensity (Wallrabe and Periasamy, 2005; Jares-Erijman and Jovin, 2003).
evidence: This is cited as an advantage of FLIM over ratiometric FRET.

claim: Occurrence of FRET leads to quenching of the donor signal, which in turn shortens its fluorescence lifetime.
source: Occurrence of FRET leads to quenching of the donor signal, which in turn shortens its fluorescence lifetime.
evidence: This is the fundamental principle underlying FRET-FLIM measurements.

claim: Reductions in the donor's lifetime reflect interactions between the proteins conjugated to the donor and acceptor fluorophores.
source: Therefore, reductions in the donor's lifetime reflect interactions between the proteins conjugated to the donor and acceptor fluorophores.
evidence: This is the interpretation of FRET-FLIM data.

claim: Dendritic cells are leukocytes essential for the activation of T cells.
source: Dendritic cells are leukocytes essential for the activation of T cells (Banchereau and Steinman, 1998).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about dendritic cells.

claim: Activation of dendritic cells by inflammatory or pathogenic stimuli triggers the production and release of cytokines and chemokines that orchestrate the immune response.
source: Activation of dendritic cells by inflammatory or pathogenic stimuli triggers the production and release of cytokines and chemokines that orchestrate the immune response (Collins et al., 2015; Stanley and Lacy, 2010).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about dendritic cell function.

claim: Not much is known about the trafficking pathways involved in cytokine release by dendritic cells.
source: Despite many studies characterizing the cytokines that are released by dendritic cells and their mechanisms of action, not much is known about the trafficking pathways involved.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Both VAMP3 and VAMP8 are associated with cytokine release from immune cells.
source: While both VAMP3 and VAMP8 are associated with cytokine release from immune cells (Collins et al., 2015; Stow et al., 2009; Stanley and Lacy, 2010; Lacy and Stow, 2011; Murray and Stow, 2014), VAMP3 is mostly associated with early and recycling endosomes and VAMP8 with late endosomes (Bajno et al., 2000; Manderson et al., 2007; Hong, 2005; Murray et al., 2005; Antonin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: VAMP3 is mostly associated with early and recycling endosomes.
source: While both VAMP3 and VAMP8 are associated with cytokine release from immune cells (Collins et al., 2015; Stow et al., 2009; Stanley and Lacy, 2010; Lacy and Stow, 2011; Murray and Stow, 2014), VAMP3 is mostly associated with early and recycling endosomes and VAMP8 with late endosomes (Bajno et al., 2000; Manderson et al., 2007; Hong, 2005; Murray et al., 2005; Antonin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: VAMP8 is associated with late endosomes.
source: While both VAMP3 and VAMP8 are associated with cytokine release from immune cells (Collins et al., 2015; Stow et al., 2009; Stanley and Lacy, 2010; Lacy and Stow, 2011; Murray and Stow, 2014), VAMP3 is mostly associated with early and recycling endosomes and VAMP8 with late endosomes (Bajno et al., 2000; Manderson et al., 2007; Hong, 2005; Murray et al., 2005; Antonin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: VAMP8 has been reported to inhibit phagocytosis by dendritic cells.
source: VAMP8 has also been reported to inhibit phagocytosis by dendritic cells (Ho et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Stx3 and Stx4 are mainly plasma membrane localized SNAREs mediating exocytosis.
source: Stx3 and Stx4 are mainly plasma membrane localized SNAREs mediating exocytosis, but also have intracellular roles in immune cells (Naegelen et al., 2015; Collins et al., 2014; Stow et al., 2009; Stanley and Lacy, 2010; Lacy and Stow, 2011; Murray and Stow, 2014; Gómez-Jaramillo et al., 2014; Frank et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Stx3 and Stx4 have intracellular roles in immune cells.
source: Stx3 and Stx4 are mainly plasma membrane localized SNAREs mediating exocytosis, but also have intracellular roles in immune cells (Naegelen et al., 2015; Collins et al., 2014; Stow et al., 2009; Stanley and Lacy, 2010; Lacy and Stow, 2011; Murray and Stow, 2014; Gómez-Jaramillo et al., 2014; Frank et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: FRET-FLIM experiments revealed FRET of fluorescently labeled Stx3 with VAMP3 in live dendritic cells predominantly at the plasma membrane.
source: Our FRET-FLIM experiments revealed FRET of fluorescently labeled Stx3 with VAMP3 in live dendritic cells and this was predominantly present at the plasma membrane, indicative of increased Stx3-VAMP3 complexing at this site.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM data shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: FRET of fluorescently labeled Stx3 with VAMP8 was higher at intracellular compartments.
source: In contrast, FRET of fluorescently labeled Stx3 with VAMP8 was higher at intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: LPS promotes the complex formation of Stx4 with VAMP3.
source: Our results also showed an increase in FRET of fluorescently labeled Stx4, but not of Stx3, with VAMP3 upon cellular activation with the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) agonist lipopolysaccharide (LPS), indicating that LPS promotes the complex formation of Stx4 with VAMP3.
evidence: This is supported by FLIM data shown in Figure 5.

claim: LPS activation of dendritic cells induces an inflammatory response characterized by the secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6.
source: LPS activation of dendritic cells induces an inflammatory response, which is characterized by the secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6) (Stow et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about LPS-induced dendritic cell activation.

claim: VAMP3 plays a key role in IL-6 secretion from dendritic cells.
source: VAMP3 plays a key role in this cytokine secretion, as siRNA knockdown of VAMP3 resulted in impaired release of IL-6 from dendritic cells.
evidence: This is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments and IL-6 ELISA data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: siRNA knockdown of VAMP3 resulted in impaired release of IL-6 from dendritic cells.
source: VAMP3 plays a key role in this cytokine secretion, as siRNA knockdown of VAMP3 resulted in impaired release of IL-6 from dendritic cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The secretion of IL-6 is regulated at the level of SNARE complex formation.
source: Our study demonstrates that the secretion of IL-6 is regulated at the level of SNARE complex formation and proves the use of FRET-FLIM for quantitative visualization of SNARE interactions in live cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the correlation between increased Stx4-VAMP3 complex formation and IL-6 secretion.

claim: mCitrine and mCherry are a suitable donor-acceptor pair for FRET because the emission spectrum of mCitrine overlaps with the excitation spectrum of mCherry.
source: The emission spectrum of mCitrine overlaps with the excitation spectrum of mCherry which makes them a suitable donor-acceptor pair for FRET (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by spectral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both mCitrine and mCherry are pH-insensitive and therefore their fluorescence lifetimes are not affected by low pH within the lumen of intracellular compartments.
source: Both mCitrine and mCherry are pH-insensitive and therefore their fluorescence lifetimes are not affected by low pH within the lumen of intracellular compartments (Griesbeck et al., 2001; Shaner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations of the original fluorescent protein characterization papers.

claim: mCitrine and mCherry are monomeric which is important to prevent oligomerization artifacts.
source: In addition, they are monomeric which is important to prevent oligomerization artifacts.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the fluorophores that makes them suitable for FRET studies.

claim: Modeling the crystal structure of the neuronal cis-SNARE complex with mCitrine and mCherry fused to C-termini of VAMP2 and Stx1 showed that these fluorophores are immediately juxtaposed to each other.
source: Modeling the crystal structure of the neuronal cis-SNARE complex (Stein et al., 2009) with mCitrine (Ho et al., 2008) and mCherry (Shu et al., 2006) fused to C-termini of VAMP2 and Stx1 showed that these fluorophores are immediately juxtaposed to each other (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 1A.

claim: mCitrine and mCherry attached to the C-termini of VAMP3 or VAMP8 and Stx3 or Stx4 would be in close proximity in a cis-SNARE complex and result in FRET and a decrease of the donor fluorescence lifetime.
source: Based on the high structural homology of SNARE proteins, we expected that mCitrine and mCherry attached to the C-termini of VAMP3 or VAMP8 and Stx3 or Stx4 would also be in close proximity in a cis-SNARE complex and that this would result in FRET and a decrease of the donor (mCitrine) fluorescence lifetime (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural homology and is tested in the experiments.

claim: Stx3-mCitrine localized to the plasma membrane and to intracellular compartments.
source: Stx3-mCitrine localized to the plasma membrane and to intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is observed in confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VAMP3-mCherry was predominantly present in intracellular compartments with only a small fraction located at the plasma membrane similar to the localization of endogenous VAMP3.
source: VAMP3-mCherry was predominantly present in intracellular compartments with only a small fraction located at the plasma membrane similar to the localization of endogenous VAMP3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in confocal microscopy images and compared to immunofluorescence of endogenous VAMP3.

claim: On average ~750,000 photons per cell were accumulated in FLIM recordings.
source: We recorded fluorescent lifetime images of live (unfixed) cells at an image plane locating at the height of the nucleus and accumulated on average ~750,000 photons per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated as a technical detail of the FLIM measurements and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cells co-transfected with Stx3-mCitrine and VAMP3-mCherry showed a reduction of the donor's apparent lifetime compared to cells expressing only Stx3-mCitrine.
source: Compared to cells expressing only Stx3-mCitrine, the FLIM images of cells co-transfected with Stx3-mCitrine and VAMP3-mCherry showed a reduction of the donor's apparent lifetime.
evidence: This is observed in FLIM images shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The lowest apparent lifetime of Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry was present at the plasma membrane.
source: The lowest apparent lifetime was present at the plasma membrane (quantification below), indicating that the complexing of VAMP3 with Stx3 mainly took place at the cell membrane and less at intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is observed in FLIM images and quantified in Figure 2E.

claim: The complexing of VAMP3 with Stx3 mainly took place at the cell membrane and less at intracellular compartments.
source: The lowest apparent lifetime was present at the plasma membrane (quantification below), indicating that the complexing of VAMP3 with Stx3 mainly took place at the cell membrane and less at intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of FRET shown in FLIM images.

claim: Co-expression of Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry resulted in a shift of the phasor location compared to the condition with the donor fluorophore only.
source: FRET was also clear from Phasor analysis (Hinde et al., 2012), as co-expression of Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry resulted in a shift of the phasor location compared to the condition with the donor fluorophore only (Stx3-mCitrine) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown in phasor plots in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The colocalization of the mCitrine and mCherry signals in the Stx3-mCitrine-mCherry tandem construct was apparent but not complete.
source: Although the colocalization of the mCitrine and mCherry signals was apparent, the overlap was not complete and the mCherry signal was more present in a cellular area juxtaposed to the nucleus (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is observed in confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: The mCherry signal was more present in a cellular area juxtaposed to the nucleus in the Stx3-mCitrine-mCherry tandem construct.
source: Although the colocalization of the mCitrine and mCherry signals was apparent, the overlap was not complete and the mCherry signal was more present in a cellular area juxtaposed to the nucleus (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is observed in confocal microscopy images.

claim: The mCherry signals were more prevalent than mCitrine in a juxtanuclear area when co-expressing VAMP3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry or VAMP8-mCitrine with VAMP8-mCherry.
source: To investigate this phenomenon further, we co-expressed VAMP3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry or VAMP8-mCitrine with VAMP8-mCherry and compared the localization of these constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I). Also in this case, the mCherry signals were more prevalent than mCitrine in a juxtanuclear area.
evidence: This is observed in confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The juxtanuclear accumulation of mCherry was also observed upon dissipating the proton gradients by paraformaldehyde fixation.
source: This juxtanuclear accumulation of mCherry was also observed upon dissipating the proton gradients by paraformaldehyde fixation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and J), indicating that the differential localization of mCherry and mCitrine was not caused by pH-quenching of mCitrine, but possibly due to differences in maturation speed or stability of the used fluorophores (Griesbeck et al., 2001; Shaner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is observed in fixed cell images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and J.

claim: The differential localization of mCherry and mCitrine was not caused by pH-quenching of mCitrine.
source: This juxtanuclear accumulation of mCherry was also observed upon dissipating the proton gradients by paraformaldehyde fixation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and J), indicating that the differential localization of mCherry and mCitrine was not caused by pH-quenching of mCitrine, but possibly due to differences in maturation speed or stability of the used fluorophores (Griesbeck et al., 2001; Shaner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fixation did not eliminate the differential localization.

claim: The differential localization of mCherry and mCitrine was possibly due to differences in maturation speed or stability of the used fluorophores.
source: This juxtanuclear accumulation of mCherry was also observed upon dissipating the proton gradients by paraformaldehyde fixation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and J), indicating that the differential localization of mCherry and mCitrine was not caused by pH-quenching of mCitrine, but possibly due to differences in maturation speed or stability of the used fluorophores (Griesbeck et al., 2001; Shaner et al., 2004).
evidence: This is speculation based on known properties of fluorescent proteins.

claim: The FRET-FLIM approach likely underestimates the amount of FRET in juxtanuclear regions.
source: Consequently, our FRET-FLIM approach likely underestimates the amount of FRET in juxtanuclear regions and more stable or rapidly maturating YFP analogs need to be developed for this.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential localization of mCherry and mCitrine.

claim: Clear overlap of mCherry and mCitrine was observed in more peripheral cellular regions with Pearson correlation coefficients between 0.6–0.8 for the whole cell.
source: However, we observed clear overlap of mCherry and mCitrine in more peripheral cellular regions (Pearson correlation coefficients between 0.6–0.8 for the whole cell; Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and K), supporting the conclusion that our FRET-FLIM method can report on SNARE interactions in those regions.
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and K.

claim: Co-transfection of Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry significantly reduced the apparent lifetime of mCitrine from 2.79 ± 0.02 ns to 2.49 ± 0.03 ns.
source: In Stx3-mCitrine expressing cells, co-transfection with VAMP3-mCherry significantly reduced the apparent lifetime of mCitrine from 2.79 ± 0.02 ns to 2.49 ± 0.03 ns (mean ± SEM) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is quantified from whole-cell fluorescence lifetime analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The spread of apparent lifetimes for cells co-expressing Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry was quite large, ranging from 2 to 3 ns.
source: The spread of apparent lifetimes for cells co-expressing Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry was quite large, ranging from 2 to 3 ns (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The large spread in apparent lifetimes was at least partly caused by the availability of VAMP3-mCherry and competition with endogenous SNAREs.
source: This large spread was at least partly caused by the availability of VAMP3-mCherry and competition with endogenous SNAREs, because the fluorescence lifetimes inversely correlated with the expression levels of VAMP3-mCherry (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The fluorescence lifetimes inversely correlated with the expression levels of VAMP3-mCherry.
source: This large spread was at least partly caused by the availability of VAMP3-mCherry and competition with endogenous SNAREs, because the fluorescence lifetimes inversely correlated with the expression levels of VAMP3-mCherry (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Most cells showed a lower apparent lifetime at the cellular periphery compared to the intracellular region.
source: Most cells showed a lower apparent lifetime at the cellular periphery compared to the intracellular region (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis in Figure 2E.

claim: The reduction in apparent lifetime between periphery and intracellular regions was on average 55 ps.
source: This reduction was on average 55 ps (paired two-sided Student's t-test; p=0.0078), but was larger for cells with higher FRET (linear regression: β = 1.18, R2 = 0.82).
evidence: This is quantified from the data in Figure 2E.

claim: The reduction in apparent lifetime between periphery and intracellular regions was larger for cells with higher FRET.
source: This reduction was on average 55 ps (paired two-sided Student's t-test; p=0.0078), but was larger for cells with higher FRET (linear regression: β = 1.18, R2 = 0.82).
evidence: This is shown by linear regression analysis of the data in Figure 2E.

claim: Co-expression of Stx3-mCitrine and VAMP3-mCherry results in a mixed population, with part of Stx3-mCitrine interacting with VAMP3-mCherry and the remainder free or engaged with endogenous VAMP3 or other R SNAREs.
source: The co-expression of Stx3-mCitrine and VAMP3-mCherry will result in a mixed population, with part of Stx3-mCitrine interacting with VAMP3-mCherry and the remainder free or engaged with endogenous VAMP3 or other R SNAREs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the composition of the SNARE population in transfected cells.

claim: The percentage of complexed Stx3-mCitrine correlated with the expression level of VAMP3-mCherry and reached up to almost 100% at high expression levels.
source: Using this analysis, the percentage of complexed Stx3-mCitrine again correlated with the expression level of VAMP3-mCherry, and reached up to almost 100% at high expression levels (Figure 2H; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by double-exponential fitting analysis in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Correlation of the apparent lifetimes from mono-exponential fits with the amplitudes from the bi-exponential fits resulted in a clear linear correlation.
source: Moreover, correlation of the apparent lifetimes from mono-exponential fits with the amplitudes from the bi-exponential fits resulted in a clear linear correlation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; linear regression: R2 = 0.812), demonstrating that these apparent lifetimes provide a reliable measure of the percentage FRET.
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Addition of rapamycin or the rapamycin analogue A/C Heterodimerizer resulted in a decrease of the apparent fluorescence lifetimes in cells expressing FKBP-Stx3-mCitrine or FKBP-Stx4-mCitrine together with FRB-VAMP3-mCherry.
source: Indeed, addition of rapamycin or the rapamycin analogue A/C Heterodimerizer resulted in a decrease of the apparent fluorescence lifetimes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in the FLIM data in Figure 3A.

claim: Deletion of leucine 71 in VAMP3 impairs membrane fusion.
source: For VAMP3, deletion of leucine 71 also impairs membrane fusion, as cells co-expressing Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3(Δ71)-mCherry showed a significantly higher apparent fluorescence lifetime compared to cells expressing non-mutant VAMP3-mCherry (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the higher apparent lifetime indicating less FRET/complex formation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cells co-expressing Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3(Δ71)-mCherry showed a significantly higher apparent fluorescence lifetime compared to cells expressing non-mutant VAMP3-mCherry.
source: For VAMP3, deletion of leucine 71 also impairs membrane fusion, as cells co-expressing Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3(Δ71)-mCherry showed a significantly higher apparent fluorescence lifetime compared to cells expressing non-mutant VAMP3-mCherry (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the FLIM data in Figure 3C.

claim: FRET-FLIM allows detection of SNARE complexes.
source: These data confirm that FRET-FLIM allows detection of SNARE complexes.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the validation experiments with rapamycin and the VAMP3 deletion mutant.

claim: Stx4-mCitrine mainly localized to the plasma membrane and only somewhat to intracellular compartments.
source: Stx4-mCitrine mainly localized to the plasma membrane and only somewhat to intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is observed in confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of VAMP8-mCherry was present in intracellular compartments.
source: Similar to VAMP3-mCherry, the majority of VAMP8-mCherry was present in intracellular compartments (Figure 4A) and this corresponded to the localization of endogenous VAMP8 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is observed in confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 4A and compared to endogenous VAMP8 in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Whole-cell fluorescence lifetime analysis revealed interactions between all SNARE pairs tested.
source: Whole-cell fluorescence lifetime analysis revealed interactions between all SNARE pairs tested, as reflected by reductions of the apparent fluorescence lifetime of mCitrine in the presence of mCherry-fused VAMP3 or VAMP8, although for Stx4 these reductions were relatively small (<100 ps) and not significant when analyzing donor-averaged lifetimes (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the FLIM data in Figure 4B.

claim: For Stx4, the reductions in apparent fluorescence lifetime were relatively small (<100 ps) and not significant when analyzing donor-averaged lifetimes.
source: Whole-cell fluorescence lifetime analysis revealed interactions between all SNARE pairs tested, as reflected by reductions of the apparent fluorescence lifetime of mCitrine in the presence of mCherry-fused VAMP3 or VAMP8, although for Stx4 these reductions were relatively small (<100 ps) and not significant when analyzing donor-averaged lifetimes (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the FLIM data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Interactions of Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry mainly occurred at the plasma membrane.
source: FLIM imaging showed that whereas interactions of Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry mainly occurred at the plasma membrane, the interactions with VAMP8-mCherry predominantly occurred at intracellular compartments (Figure 1C, Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in FLIM images shown in Figure 1C and Figure 4A.

claim: Interactions of Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP8-mCherry predominantly occurred at intracellular compartments.
source: FLIM imaging showed that whereas interactions of Stx3-mCitrine with VAMP3-mCherry mainly occurred at the plasma membrane, the interactions with VAMP8-mCherry predominantly occurred at intracellular compartments (Figure 1C, Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in FLIM images shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Addition of NEM resulted in a trend showing further reductions of the apparent fluorescence lifetimes for all combinations of donor and acceptor SNAREs tested.
source: As a positive control, we treated our cells with N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), which impairs the AAA-ATPase NSF responsible for dissociation of SNARE complexes. Addition of this compound traps all SNARE complexes in their cis-conformation (Söllner et al., 1993) and resulted in a trend showing further reductions of the apparent fluorescence lifetimes for all combinations of donor and acceptor SNAREs tested (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in the FLIM data in Figure 4B.

claim: NEM impairs the AAA-ATPase NSF responsible for dissociation of SNARE complexes and traps all SNARE complexes in their cis-conformation.
source: As a positive control, we treated our cells with N-ethylmaleimide (NEM), which impairs the AAA-ATPase NSF responsible for dissociation of SNARE complexes. Addition of this compound traps all SNARE complexes in their cis-conformation (Söllner et al., 1993) and resulted in a trend showing further reductions of the apparent fluorescence lifetimes for all combinations of donor and acceptor SNAREs tested (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is cited as the known mechanism of NEM action.

claim: FRET at the plasma membrane of fluorescently-labeled VAMP3 with Stx3 was higher than with Stx4 in unstimulated dendritic cells.
source: Thus, our FLIM data resulted in two new observations of SNARE complex formation in unstimulated dendritic cells: (i) FRET at the plasma membrane of fluorescently-labeled VAMP3 with Stx3 was higher than with Stx4, suggesting more interactions of VAMP3 with Stx3 even though most Stx4 is present at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is concluded from the FLIM data comparing different SNARE pairs.

claim: FRET of fluorescently-labeled Stx3, but not Stx4, with VAMP3 was observed mainly at the plasma membrane while FRET with VAMP8 was found mainly at intracellular compartments.
source: (ii) FRET of fluorescently-labeled Stx3, but not Stx4, with VAMP3 was observed mainly at the plasma membrane while FRET with VAMP8 was found mainly at intracellular compartments, indicating that complex formation of these SNAREs occurred in different subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is concluded from the spatial distribution of FRET in FLIM images.

claim: Complex formation of Stx3 with VAMP3 and VAMP8 occurred in different subcellular compartments.
source: (ii) FRET of fluorescently-labeled Stx3, but not Stx4, with VAMP3 was observed mainly at the plasma membrane while FRET with VAMP8 was found mainly at intracellular compartments, indicating that complex formation of these SNAREs occurred in different subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential spatial distribution of FRET.

claim: Activation of dendritic cells by inflammatory stimuli triggers the production and secretion of immunomodulatory cytokines and alters the surface receptors displayed on the cell membrane.
source: Activation of dendritic cells by inflammatory stimuli triggers the production and secretion of immunomodulatory cytokines and alters the surface receptors displayed on the cell membrane and this is accompanied by marked changes of the membrane trafficking machinery (Collins et al., 2015; Stow et al., 2009; Stanley and Lacy, 2010; Lacy and Stow, 2011; Murray and Stow, 2014; Murray et al., 2005; Pagan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about dendritic cell activation.

claim: Activation of dendritic cells is accompanied by marked changes of the membrane trafficking machinery.
source: Activation of dendritic cells by inflammatory stimuli triggers the production and secretion of immunomodulatory cytokines and alters the surface receptors displayed on the cell membrane and this is accompanied by marked changes of the membrane trafficking machinery (Collins et al., 2015; Stow et al., 2009; Stanley and Lacy, 2010; Lacy and Stow, 2011; Murray and Stow, 2014; Murray et al., 2005; Pagan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge.

claim: LPS is a component from the outer cell membrane of gram-negative bacteria and a strong agonist of TLR4.
source: We transfected dendritic cells with combinations of SNAREs and stimulated the cells overnight with the bacterial antigen LPS, a component from the outer cell membrane of gram-negative bacteria and a strong agonist of TLR4 (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LPS.

claim: TLR4 stimulation triggers danger signaling in dendritic cells leading to cell maturation characterized by a strong increase in cytokine production.
source: TLR4 stimulation triggers danger signaling in dendritic cells leading to cell maturation characterized by a strong increase in cytokine production.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TLR4 signaling.

claim: LPS stimulation can upregulate the expression of several SNAREs in immune cells.
source: Although LPS stimulation can upregulate the expression of several SNAREs in immune cells (Chiaruttini et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2005; Collins et al., 2014; Ho et al, 2009; Pagan et al., 2003), the protein levels of both endogenous and overexpressed Stx3, Stx4, VAMP3 and VAMP8 in monocyte-derived dendritic cells were not altered by LPS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is cited as known from previous studies.

claim: The protein levels of both endogenous and overexpressed Stx3, Stx4, VAMP3 and VAMP8 in monocyte-derived dendritic cells were not altered by LPS.
source: Although LPS stimulation can upregulate the expression of several SNAREs in immune cells (Chiaruttini et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2005; Collins et al., 2014; Ho et al, 2009; Pagan et al., 2003), the protein levels of both endogenous and overexpressed Stx3, Stx4, VAMP3 and VAMP8 in monocyte-derived dendritic cells were not altered by LPS (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: LPS activation of dendritic cells expressing Stx4-mCitrine in combination with VAMP3-mCherry led to a significant reduction of the apparent lifetime compared to the condition without LPS.
source: Whole-cell FLIM analysis revealed that LPS activation of dendritic cells expressing Stx4-mCitrine in combination with VAMP3-mCherry led to a significant reduction of the apparent lifetime compared to the condition without LPS (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the FLIM data in Figure 5B.

claim: No significant changes in apparent lifetime were observed for Stx3-mCitrine or for VAMP8-mCherry upon LPS activation.
source: In contrast, no significant changes were observed for Stx3-mCitrine or for VAMP8-mCherry.
evidence: This is shown in the FLIM data in Figure 5B.

claim: The interactions of VAMP3-mCherry with Stx4-mCitrine mainly occurred at the plasma membrane upon LPS activation.
source: FLIM imaging demonstrated that the interactions of VAMP3-mCherry with Stx4-mCitrine mainly occurred at the plasma membrane (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in FLIM images shown in Figure 5A.

claim: VAMP3 is known to mediate release of inflammatory cytokines by the murine macrophage cell line RAW264.7.
source: VAMP3 is known to mediate release of inflammatory cytokines by the murine macrophage cell line RAW264.7 (Manderson et al., 2007) and the human synovial sarcoma cell line SW982 (Boddul et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: VAMP3 is known to mediate release of inflammatory cytokines by the human synovial sarcoma cell line SW982.
source: VAMP3 is known to mediate release of inflammatory cytokines by the murine macrophage cell line RAW264.7 (Manderson et al., 2007) and the human synovial sarcoma cell line SW982 (Boddul et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: VAMP3 is required for the secretion of cytokines by LPS activated monocyte-derived dendritic cells.
source: VAMP3 is also required for the secretion of cytokines by LPS activated monocyte-derived dendritic cells, as siRNA knockdown of this SNARE impaired release of the cytokine IL-6, as shown by ELISA (Figure 5C–D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown by siRNA knockdown experiments and ELISA data in Figure 5C-D.

claim: LPS activation of dendritic cells results in an increased complex formation of Stx4 with VAMP3 at the plasma membrane and this promotes IL-6 secretion.
source: These FLIM data support the conclusion that LPS activation of dendritic cells results in an increased complex formation of Stx4 with VAMP3 at the plasma membrane and that this promotes IL-6 secretion.
evidence: This conclusion integrates the FLIM data showing increased Stx4-VAMP3 FRET with the IL-6 secretion data.

claim: FRET-FLIM enables the assignment of SNARE partners to specific trafficking routes.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that FRET-FLIM enables the assignment of SNARE partners to specific trafficking routes, as it allows visualization of SNARE pairing at subcellular resolution.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: FLIM-FRET is a quantitative method that in principle allows to determine the fraction of SNAREs engaged in complex formation by fitting the photon counts with bi-exponential decay functions with fixed lifetimes.
source: Our data show that FLIM-FRET is a quantitative method that in principle allows to determine the fraction of SNAREs engaged in complex formation by fitting the photon counts with bi-exponential decay functions with fixed lifetimes (i.e., for no FRET (donor only) and 100% FRET (all SNAREs interacting)).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the double-exponential fitting analysis shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: Fusing chromosomal SNARE-encoding genes with fluorescent proteins using CRISPR/CAS9 in cell lines will enable quantification of endogenous SNARE interactions by FRET-FLIM.
source: While the transient overexpression system used for our primary cells does not allow meaningful quantification of SNARE complexing, we expect that fusing chromosomal SNARE-encoding genes with fluorescent proteins using CRISPR/CAS9 in cell lines will enable to quantify endogenous SNARE interactions by FRET-FLIM.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: In unstimulated dendritic cells, the apparent lifetime of fluorescently labeled Stx3 with VAMP3 was lower at the periphery of the imaged cell areas, whereas the apparent lifetime with VAMP8 was lower at intracellular areas.
source: In unstimulated dendritic cells, the apparent lifetime of fluorescently labeled Stx3 with VAMP3 was lower at the periphery of the imaged cell areas, whereas the apparent lifetime with VAMP8 was lower at intracellular areas.
evidence: This is observed in the FLIM data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 4.

claim: Complex formation of Stx3 with VAMP3 mainly occurs at the plasma membrane, while interactions with VAMP8 predominantly occur at intracellular compartments.
source: This indicates that complex formation of Stx3 with VAMP3 mainly occurs at the plasma membrane, while interactions with VAMP8 predominantly occur at intracellular compartments.
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial distribution of FRET.

claim: VAMP3 is primarily localized in early and recycling endosomes.
source: VAMP3 is primarily localized in early and recycling endosomes and VAMP8 locates predominately at late endosomal compartments (Bajno et al., 2000; Manderson et al., 2007; Hong, 2005; Antonin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge.

claim: VAMP8 locates predominately at late endosomal compartments.
source: VAMP3 is primarily localized in early and recycling endosomes and VAMP8 locates predominately at late endosomal compartments (Bajno et al., 2000; Manderson et al., 2007; Hong, 2005; Antonin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge.

claim: Fusion of compartments of early/recycling endosomal nature with the plasma membrane is more abundant than of late endosomal compartments.
source: Our data are therefore perfectly in line with the widely accepted notion that fusion of compartments of early/recycling endosomal nature with the plasma membrane is more abundant than of late endosomal compartments.
evidence: This is stated as consistent with established knowledge and supported by the FLIM data.

claim: The interactions of VAMP3 at the plasma membrane with Stx4 are lower than with Stx3 in unstimulated dendritic cells.
source: Based on differences in apparent fluorescence lifetimes, we also conclude that the interactions of VAMP3 at the plasma membrane with Stx4 are lower than with Stx3 in unstimulated dendritic cells, even though the vast majority of Stx4 is present at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing apparent lifetimes in the FLIM data.

claim: LPS triggers increased exocytosis by VAMP3 and Stx4.
source: This result indicates that LPS triggers increased exocytosis by VAMP3 and Stx4.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased FRET between Stx4 and VAMP3 upon LPS treatment.

claim: Many cytokines traffic via recycling endosomes to the plasma membrane, including IL-6 and TNFα.
source: VAMP3 is a recycling endosomal SNARE (Bajno et al., 2000; Manderson et al., 2007; Hong, 2005; Murray et al., 2005) and many cytokines traffic via recycling endosomes to the plasma membrane, including IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (Manderson et al., 2007; Murray et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge.

claim: siRNA knockdown of VAMP3 impairs IL-6 secretion by monocyte-derived dendritic cells as previously observed for RAW264.7 murine macrophages and SW982 human synovial sarcoma cells.
source: Indeed, our data show that siRNA knockdown of VAMP3 impairs IL-6 secretion by monocyte-derived dendritic cells as previously observed for RAW264.7 murine macrophages (Manderson et al., 2007) and SW982 human synovial sarcoma cells (Boddul et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown by the experimental data in Figure 5C-D and compared to cited previous studies.

claim: The increased complexing of VAMP3 with Stx4 is likely responsible for the increased secretion of IL-6 and other cytokines by activated dendritic cells.
source: As supported by our FRET-FLIM data the increased complexing of VAMP3 with Stx4 is thus likely responsible for the increased secretion of IL-6 and other cytokines by activated dendritic cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between increased Stx4-VAMP3 FRET and IL-6 secretion.

claim: LPS increased FRET only of VAMP3 with Stx4 and not with Stx3.
source: Interestingly, we observed that LPS increased FRET only of VAMP3 with Stx4 and not with Stx3.
evidence: This is shown in the FLIM data in Figure 5B.

claim: Stx3 and Stx4 catalyze apical and basolateral exocytosis respectively in epithelial cells.
source: Stx3 and Stx4 have been well described in epithelial cells, where they catalyze apical and basolateral exocytosis respectively (Low et al., 1996; ter Beest et al., 2005; Procino et al., 2008), but why non-polarized cells such as dendritic cells express both syntaxins is not well understood.
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about Stx3 and Stx4 in epithelial cells.

claim: Why non-polarized cells such as dendritic cells express both Stx3 and Stx4 is not well understood.
source: Stx3 and Stx4 have been well described in epithelial cells, where they catalyze apical and basolateral exocytosis respectively (Low et al., 1996; ter Beest et al., 2005; Procino et al., 2008), but why non-polarized cells such as dendritic cells express both syntaxins is not well understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Activation of dendritic cells leads to a rerouting of intracellular trafficking with more VAMP3-containing compartments fusing with the plasma membrane by interacting with Stx4.
source: Our study provides a possible clue why this could be the case, as our data indicate that activation of the dendritic cells leads to a rerouting of intracellular trafficking with more VAMP3-containing compartments fusing with the plasma membrane by interacting with Stx4.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased Stx4-VAMP3 FRET upon LPS activation.

claim: Stx3 catalyzes the constitutive cycling of early/recycling endosomes in resting cells and Stx4 offers the spare capacity to fulfil the additional secretory requirements upon dendritic cell activation.
source: Perhaps Stx3 catalyzes the constitutive cycling of early/recycling endosomes in resting cells and Stx4 offers the spare capacity to fulfil the additional secretory requirements upon dendritic cell activation needed for the secretion of massive amounts of cytokines.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differential regulation of Stx3 and Stx4.

claim: The increased SNARE complexing upon dendritic cell activation is not caused by increased levels of Stx4 or VAMP3.
source: What could cause the increased Stx4 complex formation with VAMP3 upon dendritic cell activation? Our data show that such increased SNARE complexing is not caused by increased levels of Stx4 or VAMP3.
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The increased complexing might be regulated by direct phosphorylation of Stx4, VAMP3 and/or SNAP23.
source: Possibly, the increased complexing might be regulated by direct phosphorylation of Stx4, VAMP3 and/or the Qb/c-SNARE SNAP23 (Malmersjö et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation with a supporting citation.

claim: SNAP23 was recently shown to be phosphorylated in an IκB-kinase two dependent fashion upon stimulation of mouse dendritic cells with LPS.
source: SNAP23 was recently shown to be phosphorylated in an IκB-kinase two dependent fashion upon stimulation of mouse dendritic cells with LPS and this mediates the delivery of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I from recycling endosomes to phagosomes, presumably via Stx4 and VAMP3 or VAMP8 (Nair-Gupta et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is cited from a recent study.

claim: Phosphorylation of SNAP23 mediates the delivery of MHC class I from recycling endosomes to phagosomes, presumably via Stx4 and VAMP3 or VAMP8.
source: SNAP23 was recently shown to be phosphorylated in an IκB-kinase two dependent fashion upon stimulation of mouse dendritic cells with LPS and this mediates the delivery of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I from recycling endosomes to phagosomes, presumably via Stx4 and VAMP3 or VAMP8 (Nair-Gupta et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is cited from a recent study.

claim: The increased complex formation could be regulated by the Sec1/Munc18-protein Munc18c (STXBP3).
source: Alternatively, or additionally, the increased complex formation could be regulated by the Sec1/Munc18-protein Munc18c (STXBP3).
evidence: This is speculation about possible regulatory mechanisms.

claim: Munc18c and Stx4 are well known to regulate GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes and skeletal muscle cells.
source: Munc18c and Stx4 are well known to regulate GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes and skeletal muscle cells (Tellam et al., 1997; Hong, 2005), and are also implied in insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells (Zhu et al., 2015), secretion of dense-core granules, α-granules and lysosomes from human platelets (Schraw et al., 2003) and TNFα secretion from macrophages (Pagan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge about Munc18c and Stx4.

claim: Munc18c and Stx4 are implied in insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells.
source: Munc18c and Stx4 are well known to regulate GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes and skeletal muscle cells (Tellam et al., 1997; Hong, 2005), and are also implied in insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells (Zhu et al., 2015), secretion of dense-core granules, α-granules and lysosomes from human platelets (Schraw et al., 2003) and TNFα secretion from macrophages (Pagan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Munc18c and Stx4 are implied in secretion of dense-core granules, α-granules and lysosomes from human platelets.
source: Munc18c and Stx4 are well known to regulate GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes and skeletal muscle cells (Tellam et al., 1997; Hong, 2005), and are also implied in insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells (Zhu et al., 2015), secretion of dense-core granules, α-granules and lysosomes from human platelets (Schraw et al., 2003) and TNFα secretion from macrophages (Pagan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Munc18c and Stx4 are implied in TNFα secretion from macrophages.
source: Munc18c and Stx4 are well known to regulate GLUT4 trafficking in adipocytes and skeletal muscle cells (Tellam et al., 1997; Hong, 2005), and are also implied in insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells (Zhu et al., 2015), secretion of dense-core granules, α-granules and lysosomes from human platelets (Schraw et al., 2003) and TNFα secretion from macrophages (Pagan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: The mechanism regulating increased Stx4-VAMP3 complex formation must be specific for Stx4 and VAMP3, as FRET of Stx3 with VAMP3 and of Stx4 with VAMP8 are not altered by LPS-activation of dendritic cells.
source: In any case, the mechanism must be specific for Stx4 and VAMP3, as our data show that FRET of Stx3 with VAMP3 and of Stx4 with VAMP8 are not altered by LPS-activation of dendritic cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity of the LPS effect shown in the FLIM data.

claim: FRET-FLIM will allow deciphering the precise intracellular trafficking pathways of molecules important in health and disease, such as cytokines, receptors, hormones, metabolic enzymes and metabolites.
source: Overall, our study demonstrates the use of FRET-FLIM for the identification of the SNARE partners orchestrating specific organellar membrane trafficking steps. We expect this technique will allow deciphering the precise intracellular trafficking pathways of molecules important in health and disease, such as cytokines, receptors, hormones, metabolic enzymes and metabolites.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the technique.
